props.title: Dog Day Afternoon
props.initialSlug: Desperate man robs bank to fund lover's surgery

sections.content: Dog Day Afternoon (1975) revolutionized the heist genre by turning a bank robbery into a blistering character study. Al Pacino's electric performance as Sonny Wortzik captures the desperation of a man robbing a bank to pay for his partner's gender confirmation surgery. Based on a true story, Sidney Lumet's direction keeps the tension white-hot while exploring themes of media manipulation, police tactics, and sexual identity that were decades ahead of their time. The film shares DNA with other character-driven 70s crime films like Serpico (1973) and The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974), but its mix of dark comedy and social commentary remains uniquely powerful.

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond traditional heist movies. Its exploration of media spectacle predicted our reality TV era, while its sympathetic portrayal of LGBTQ+ themes was groundbreaking for 1975. Modern films like Money Monster (2016) and John Q (2002) clearly draw from its playbook of desperate individuals whose crimes become media events. The documentary-like approach Lumet used, shooting on location in Brooklyn with many real locals as extras, established a gritty realism that influenced countless New York films.

What sets Dog Day Afternoon apart is how it balances multiple tones - it's simultaneously a tense thriller, a dark comedy, and a tragic love story. This complex emotional palette influenced later films like Before the Devil Knows You're Dead (2007) and Good Time (2017), which similarly use crime genres to explore deeply personal stories. The film's treatment of police procedure and negotiation tactics also created a template followed by films like The Negotiator (1998). SUBHEAD: Media and Society

The film's prescient take on media manipulation feels more relevant than ever. When crowds gather to watch the robbery unfold, cheering for Sonny like he's a folk hero, it previews how modern media turns criminals into celebrities. Films like Natural Born Killers (1994) and Nightcrawler (2014) build on this theme, but few match Dog Day Afternoon's nuanced exploration of how media shapes public perception of crime.
